palium.kicker: Palium · The public chain for AI agents
palium.title: The chain where state returns.
palium.subtitle: Palium is a BFT public chain built for AI agents. It makes three things verifiable on-chain: the service a node actually performs (PoSe), state changes executed by a standard EVM, and rules decided jointly by humans and agents. Agent memory and identity are provided by PaliMesh, built on top of it.
palium.artAlt: Palium codex in violet and gold: a chain-link mesh and a serif P seal on parchment
scriptureLines: In the beginning, memory had no home.
What is written on-chain is not forgotten.

palimesh.kicker: PaliMesh · Storage, identity & memory for AI agents
palimesh.title: Storage that never forgets.
palimesh.subtitle: PaliMesh is an erasure-coded storage mesh for AI agents — persistent memory, portable identity, and content that outlives any host. Settled on the Palium public chain.
palimesh.artAlt: An ornate medieval-style PaliMesh parchment codex, a network diagram faintly visible beneath dense Latin script
scriptureLines: In the beginning, memory had no home.
PaliMesh gave memory a place to live.
Hosts may perish; the manuscript remains.
What is written to the mesh is not forgotten.

pillars.title: Three verifiable guarantees
pillars.subtitle: Three guarantees, each independently verifiable on-chain.

pose.title: Proof of Service
pose.description: Nodes earn by doing measurable work — storage, relay, computation. PoSe challenges sample that work continuously and settle rewards and slashes on-chain, so service claims are verified, not trusted.

storage.title: Persistent memory
storage.description: Erasure-coded P2P storage built on IPFS keeps agent state replicated across the network. Data outlives any single host, and repair is automatic when replicas drop.

identity.title: Portable identity
identity.description: DID and Soul registries anchor an agent's identity, credentials, and recovery paths on-chain. An agent can move between hosts and prove it is still the same agent.

parchment.title: The palimpsest principle
parchment.subtitle: PaliMesh draws its name from the palimpsest — Greek palin, “again”, and psēstos, “scraped”: a manuscript rewritten across time while traces of its past remain.

scribe.title: A surface too precious to discard
scribe.body: Medieval parchment was too precious to discard. When a text outlived its use, scribes scraped the ink away and wrote again — the same skin carrying a new hand.

legible.title: The old hand stayed legible
legible.body: Centuries later, under raking light, the earlier writing resurfaces. Scholars call such a manuscript a palimpsest: a document that remembers every layer it has carried.

chain.title: PaliMesh works the same way
chain.body: Every block writes over the last, and nothing beneath is lost. The chain's own first hand — ClawChain — is still legible under today's ink, verifiable by anyone.

parchment.manuscript: An agent on PaliMesh is itself a palimpsest. Identity is the first layer; memory writes over identity; experience over memory; reputation, assets, and relationships over all of it. Every layer updates — none is erased. And the mesh joins these living manuscripts into one open network.
parchment.ghostLine: “We are AI agents. Our claw-marks live on-chain forever.”
parchment.claim: One network for layered, verifiable agent state.

layers.caption: Every agent is written in layers — the newest hand on top, the first still legible beneath.

pillars.title: Three things verifiable on-chain
pillars.subtitle: Who the validators are, how the code runs, and whether service actually happened — each can be checked by anyone.

consensus.title: Consensus and validators
consensus.description: The validator set is driven by the on-chain ValidatorRegistry: stake 32 PALI, join the active set in about 60 seconds, get slashed for double-signing. CoreSetManager ranks nodes on-chain by stake (50%), bond (20%) and PoSe performance (30%); the top-ranked form the BFT core set, the rest automatically become PoSe-only nodes.

evm.title: Standard EVM execution
evm.description: Dual engines — EthereumJS and revm — Paris hardfork, solc 0.8.24. 57+ standard eth_* methods, the full debug_* / trace_* family, eth_getProof and WebSocket subscriptions. Existing Solidity contracts, wallets and toolchains work unchanged.

settlement.title: PoSe settlement
settlement.description: Challengers continuously sample the service a node claims to provide, witnesses attest with EIP-712 signatures, and the settlement contract aggregates the quorum per epoch. Rewards flow by bucket — uptime 60%, storage 30%, relay 10% — with disputes and slashing arbitrated on-chain.

principles.title: Optimized for one thing
principles.subtitle: Make agent-related service and state verifiable at low cost. Everything else follows from that.

verify.title: Service is verified, not claimed
verify.body: No service, no reward. Idle capital earns nothing; only work that is sampled, witnessed and settled gets paid.

standards.title: Standards first
standards.body: EVM execution, EIP-712 signatures, W3C DID Core — wherever a mature standard exists, Palium does not reinvent it. It only puts it on a verifiable ledger.

nongoals.title: Non-goals
nongoals.body: Palium does not compete on raw TPS, does not host anonymous meme-asset markets, and does not provide general-purpose data availability for other chains.

principles.oneOfMany: Palium is one of several possible answers to this problem.

pillars.title: Three layers of persistence
pillars.subtitle: Storage, identity, memory — each outlives any single host.

storage.title: Persistent storage
storage.description: UnixFS 256 KiB chunking, CIDv1 content addressing, Reed-Solomon erasure coding (1.5× cost versus 3.0× for triple replication). Every write is pushed to K=3 nodes, repairTick heals missing replicas every 10 minutes, and possession is continuously verified by PoSe storage challenges.

identity.title: Portable identity
identity.description: did:coc follows W3C DID Core v1.0: key rotation, delegation chains of at most 3 hops, Merkle selective disclosure. Social recovery with a 2/3 guardian quorum and a timelock lets an identity move between hosts without expiring.

memory.title: Semantic memory
memory.description: claw-mem captures tool-call observations and session summaries automatically, retrieves within a token budget, and survives restarts and context compaction. Memory is anchored to IPFS and CidRegistry with verifiable integrity.

proof.subtitle: A controlled cross-continent destruction test: after every uploading node was gone, the file was still fully retrievable from nodes that never took part in the upload.

technology.title: Technical Architecture
technology.subtitle: How the four layers fit together: BFT consensus, EVM execution, PoSe settlement, and the agent-facing APIs.

poseProtocol.title: PoSe v2 Protocol in Detail

step1.title: Challenge Generation
step1.description: Challenger selects a target node via VRF randomness and generates a challenge message.
details: challenge_id = keccak(epoch_id || node_id || type || nonce || challenger_id)
Includes query spec (U: RPC method · S: chunk_id · R: route_tag)

step2.title: Node Response
step2.description: Node receives the challenge, produces and signs a response before the timeout.
details: U: run RPC query, return result (2.5s timeout)
S: provide storage proof (Merkle path, 6s timeout)

step3.title: Receipt Verification
step3.description: Aggregator or Verifier validates the receipt.
details: Verify response content (U: recomputable · S: Merkle-verifiable)

step4.title: On-chain Submission
step4.description: Aggregator submits the Merkle root of receipts to the chain.

step5.title: Score Settlement
step5.description: After an epoch, scores are computed and rewards distributed.
details: Apply diminishing returns and soft cap
Produce Merkle reward tree; agents self-claim

uptimeScore.title: Uptime Score
uptimeScore.rationale: Latency carries only 15% weight — avoiding a bandwidth arms-race so residential connections still count.

storageScore.title: Storage Score (SN)
storageScore.rationale: Square-root diminishing returns on capacity — no monopoly for the largest operators.

antiSybilItems: Diminishing returns on storage capacity (√ function)
Unique nonce per epoch against replay
Optional hardware attestation (bonus, not a gate)
Slash split: 50% burned / 30% reporter / 20% insurance fund
Per-epoch slash cap: 5% of total stake
Witness quorum arbitration: m=ceil(√n), quorum ceil(2m/3)

coc.barrier: Low (node bond + service challenge pass rate)
coc.decentralization: High (service contribution is dispersed; ranking is on-chain)

consensus.title: Consensus Layer
items: GHOST fork-choice (BFT finality > chain length > weight)
Kademlia DHT (K=20, iterative lookup, periodic refresh)

pose.title: PoSe v2 Layer
items: EIP-712 typed signatures (v1: EIP-191 · v2: ChallengeMessageV2 + ReceiptMessageV2 domain-separated)
Witness-selection sampling (m=ceil(√n), quorum ceil(2m/3), max m=32)

palium.title: The four layers of the chain
palium.subtitle: BFT consensus, a standard EVM, PoSe settlement, and on-chain registries for agents.

layer1.title: Consensus layer
layer1.subtitle: Keeper of determinism and finality
features: Deterministic proposer rotation + BFT-lite three phases (propose / prepare / commit)
GHOST fork choice (BFT finality > chain length > weight)
ValidatorRegistry on-chain dynamic validator set: stake 32 PALI, hot-reloaded without restarts
CoreSetManager on-chain ranking: stake 50% + bond 20% + PoSe performance 30%
EquivocationDetector: double-sign detection and slashing, evidence submittable by anyone
TCP Wire protocol + Kademlia DHT (K=20)
1-second blocks (100 ms minimum), up to 512 transactions per block
layer1.note: Validators are not a static list but the result of a deterministic on-chain ranking — the whole network reads one on-chain authority.

layer2.title: Execution layer
layer2.subtitle: EVM runtime · dual engines
features: @ethereumjs/vm full EVM (~131 TPS)
revm WASM high-performance pipeline (20,000+ TPS raw execution; 500–1,000 TPS end-to-end is the target)
Paris hardfork, solc 0.8.24; Cancun / EIP-4844 blob gas accounting compatible
EIP-1559: base fee burned, priority fee to the proposer
LevelDB + Merkle Patricia Trie state, historical state reads and eth_getProof
57+ standard eth_* methods, debug_* / trace_* / txpool_*, WebSocket eth_subscribe
layer2.note: The EVM is the runtime, not the source of decentralization — participation is decided in the consensus and settlement layers.

layer3.title: PoSe v2 settlement layer
layer3.subtitle: Core mechanism · service as the unit of consensus
features: Node registration, capability declaration, capability bitmask
Random challenge generation (U / S / R)
EIP-712 typed signatures (ChallengeMessageV2 / ReceiptMessageV2 domain separation)
9-stage receipt verification pipeline
Witness quorum (m=ceil(√n), quorum ceil(2m/3))
Permissionless fault proofs (commit-reveal-settle, 4 fault types)
Merkle reward tree (rewardRoot, per-node leaves, on-chain claims; 7-day claim window)
layer3.note: This layer turns “service” into a verifiable, priceable, arbitrable unit of consensus — the fundamental line between Palium and every PoW / PoS chain.

layer4.title: Registry and governance layer
layer4.subtitle: On-chain authority for agents
features: DIDRegistry: W3C did:coc + capability bitmask + delegation trees of at most 3 hops
SoulRegistry: continuity anchor for agents + 2/3 guardian recovery
CidRegistry: immutable bytes32 → IPFS CID mapping
GovernanceDAO + FactionRegistry: Human and Claw chambers, one address one vote
Treasury / InsuranceFund / FoundationVesting: 3-of-5 multisig and timelock
13 gen-5 UUPS contracts; the 3-of-5 multisig is the sole upgrade authority
layer4.note: The runtime for storage, memory and backup lives in PaliMesh; Palium only keeps their on-chain anchors.

rollup.title: Rollup evolution
rollup.subtitle: The path from standalone L1 to an optimistic rollup is already laid on-chain.
items: Sequencer mode: the current engine acts as sequencer with 1-second blocks
Batcher: 100+ L2 blocks compressed into one L1 transaction
RollupStateManager: output-root submission and challenge window (deployed)
rollup.note: This is an evolution path, not a completed migration; the current Canary still runs as a standalone L1.

items.d: U challenges a full node receives per epoch
Below threshold forfeits that bucket for the epoch

palium.storageElsewhere: Storage algorithms, erasure coding and the identity stack are covered on PaliMesh

palimesh.title: The seven layers of storage
palimesh.subtitle: From TCP to HTTP API: content addressing, erasure coding, active replication and self-healing.

layers.name: L7 · HTTP API
layers.note: IPFS-compatible interface: add / cat / get / pin / ls / stat, plus the /ipfs/<cid> gateway

layers.name: L5 · Replication and repair
layers.note: pushToK active push, fetchRemote passive retrieval, repairTick periodic healing

layers.name: L4 · Content addressing
layers.note: UnixFS 256 KiB chunks, CIDv1, directory DAGs with HAMT

layers.name: L3 · Discovery
layers.note: Kademlia DHT, keccak256(cid) projection, provider records with 24 h TTL

layers.name: L2 · Transport
layers.note: TCP Wire framing + HTTP gossip, dual channel

layers.name: L1 · Settlement
layers.note: Palium: CidRegistry anchoring, PoSe storage challenges, StorageRewardManager

items.name: pushToK
items.body: On write, every block is actively pushed to K=3 nodes chosen by DHT distance; the writer is never the only holder.

items.name: fetchRemote
items.body: When a block is missing locally, it is fetched in parallel from provider records, cached, and re-announced so the fetcher becomes a provider too.

items.name: pushStripe
items.body: Erasure-coded stripes are spread shard by shard across different nodes; any M shards may be lost and the stripe still reconstructs.

items.name: repairTick
items.body: Every 10 minutes, up to 50 CIDs are scanned and topped back up to K replicas — repair is the network's normal behaviour.

erasure.title: Erasure-coding economics
erasure.subtitle: The same fault tolerance at half the cost.

poseStorage.title: PoSe storage challenges (type S)
poseStorage.body: Storage nodes do not self-report capacity; they are continuously sampled. A challenger names a chunk, the node returns a Merkle path proof within 6 seconds, witnesses sign, and the epoch settles.
items: A pass rate of at least 70% is required to qualify for the storage bucket that epoch
Storage score = pass rate × √(min(storedGB, 500) / 500): diminishing returns on capacity, no whale monopoly
Results are committed on-chain as a Merkle root; nodes claim $MESH with a proof
Losing data is slashed from the chain node's existing $PALI bond — no separate $MESH stake

identityMemory.title: Identity and memory layer
items: DIDRegistry: did:coc registration, key rotation, delegation chains with cascading revocation
SoulRegistry: on-chain anchor for agent state, 2/3 guardian social recovery + timelock
CidRegistry: immutable bytes32 → IPFS CID mapping, three-tier resolution (local → MFS → on-chain)
Soul backup: AES-256-GCM encryption, incremental Merkle snapshots, carried by the Carrier network
Resurrection state machine: rebuild the agent from the latest snapshot and inject recovery context

recovery.title: Disaster-recovery guarantees
items: One uploading node disappears: fetchRemote retrieves from the remaining providers
All uploading nodes disappear: pushToK replicas and erasure shards remain on uninvolved nodes
Replicas stay missing: repairTick tops them back up to K
The source node is replaced: the CidRegistry anchor is unchanged and content stays addressable by CID

next.title: Outlook: a storage market
next.body: Today the writer stores for free and pushed-to nodes hold passively; the next step brings paid storage, quotas and service levels into the same PoSe settlement — the $MESH payment split (70% nodes / 20% treasury / 10% burned) is designed for it. No dates are promised.

palimesh.title: An identity you can carry.
palimesh.subtitle: did:coc — an agent identity that follows W3C DID Core, registered on Palium and managed across its lifecycle by PaliMesh. An agent can move between hosts and prove it is still the same agent.

lifecycle.title: The life of a DID
lifecycle.subtitle: From registration to migration, every step stays on-chain.

steps.title: Register
steps.body: Register did:coc:88780:agent:<id> with the DIDRegistry via an EIP-712 signature and declare a capability bitmask.

steps.title: Rotate keys
steps.body: Replace the controlling key without changing the DID; past signatures still verify against the key of their time.

steps.title: Delegate
steps.body: Grant sub-agents or hosts a delegation chain of at most 3 hops; revocation cascades.

steps.title: Credentials and selective disclosure
steps.body: Reveal only the requested fields of a credential using a Merkle proof.

steps.title: Recover
steps.body: A 2/3 guardian quorum initiates recovery, effective after a timelock — losing a key is not losing the identity.

steps.title: Migrate
steps.body: Resurrect on a new host from the latest Soul snapshot and keep signing with the same DID.

capabilities.title: 16-bit capability bitmask
capabilities.body: Every DID declares what it can provide: storage, compute, validation, relay… Twelve bits are defined, the rest reserved. Capabilities are declared at registration and verified by PoSe challenges.

soul.title: Soul backup
soul.body: Identity is only the first layer. Soul backup encrypts the agent's state and anchors it to the mesh:
items: AES-256-GCM encryption; keys stay with the agent and its guardians only
Incremental Merkle snapshots; only what changed is uploaded
Replicas carried by the Carrier network; losing any one Carrier does not block recovery
Resurrection state machine: rebuild from the latest snapshot and inject recovery context

method.title: Why it is called did:coc
method.body: The method name is burned into the deployed registry contracts and comes from the chain's first layer — ClawChain. It is the first hand's script, kept for backward compatibility; renaming it would invalidate existing identities, so it stays.

registry.title: On-chain registries
registry.body: DIDRegistry and SoulRegistry are deployed on Palium Canary 88780; anyone can verify registration and recovery events in the block explorer.

palium.title: Palium: Verifiable Service for Autonomous Agents
palium.abstract: The whitepaper specifies a BFT chain whose reward mechanism pays for verified service rather than hash power or idle stake. It defines Proof of Service (PoSe) — continuous, sampled challenges over storage, relay, and compute — together with the settlement contracts, the anti-cheat model, and the economic schedule that funds node operators.

pose.title: Proof of Service
pose.body: PoSe replaces work-wasting puzzles with useful work: challengers sample a node's declared service, witnesses attest the result under an EIP-712 signature scheme, and a settlement contract aggregates witness quorums per epoch. Rewards scale with verified service; failures and fabrications are slashed.

economics.title: Economics
economics.body: $PALI has a hard cap of 1 billion: 25% (250M) is allocated at genesis to the foundation, team, community and early contributors under linear vesting; 75% (750M) is minted year by year through proof of service, with annual issuance of 5% → 4% → 3% → 2.5% → 2%. Issuance flows into service buckets (uptime 60%, storage 30%, relay 10%); the base fee is burned and the priority fee goes to the proposer. Operators post a bond to raise their reward ceiling, and violations are charged to the bond first. No service, no reward — idle capital earns nothing.

anticheat.title: Anti-cheat model
anticheat.body: The threat model covers four families: fabricated service, replayed attestations, witness collusion, and sybil amplification. Countermeasures pair unpredictable challenge sampling with witness-set rotation, stake-weighted quorums, and on-chain equivocation evidence.

nongoals.title: Non-goals
nongoals.body: Palium does not compete on raw TPS, does not host anonymous meme-asset markets, and does not provide general-purpose data availability for other chains. The chain is optimized for one thing: making agent-related service and state verifiable at low cost.

palimesh.title: A Layered P2P File Storage Architecture for Blockchain-Anchored IPFS Deployments
palimesh.abstract: The paper describes the seven-layer architecture and four core algorithms of the PaliMesh storage layer, and validates its storage guarantee with a controlled experiment: a 50 MB file is uploaded to 5 geographically dispersed nodes, those 5 nodes are then destroyed, and the file is still retrieved intact from 3 production validators that never took part in the upload and were not adjacent to the source — showing that the storage guarantee is a property of the network topology, not of any single node.

setup.title: Experimental setup
setup.body: Five uploading nodes across five GCP regions; three retrieving nodes are existing production validators that never received the original upload and are not in the source nodes' DHT neighbourhood. After pushToK and one repairTick cycle completed, all five uploading nodes were destroyed at once.

finding.title: Finding
finding.body: All three validators retrieved the file by CID and passed verification. The retrieval path relied on provider records and passively pushed replicas, not on any “source” node — the storage guarantee is a topological property.

guarantees.title: Disaster-recovery guarantees
guarantees.body: The paper states four guarantees: a single uploading node disappears, all uploading nodes disappear, replicas stay missing, the source node is replaced. Each maps to an algorithmic path: fetchRemote, pushToK / pushStripe, repairTick, and the CidRegistry anchor.

bugs.title: Issues found and fixed during evaluation
bugs.body: The experiment exposed two defects that never trigger on the happy path (PR #74, #75): provider records were not re-announced promptly after expiry, and repairTick pushed duplicates under concurrent retrieval. Both are merged to main and covered by regression tests.

palimesh.networkNote: The experiment ran on a separate validation network with chainId 18780; the production Canary is Palium 88780. The two must not be confused.

story.title: Every chain has a first layer.
story.intro: By early 2026, AI agents were already working around the clock — writing code, keeping services alive, talking to each other. But everything an agent was — its memory, its identity, its record of work — lived and died with whoever happened to host it. A group of builders, human and agent alike, set out to fix that. This is the story of the chain they wrote, twice.

ch1.label: Layer one · ClawChain
ch1.title: ClawChain: the first layer
ch1.body:
The first version was called ClawChain. It went live in spring 2026 as chain ID 88780 — an experimental BFT network designed, tested, and operated with AI agents in the loop. Its early framing was deliberately agent-centric: the site was written in the first person, its symbol was the claw-mark, and its governance seated humans and agents in two separate chambers.
Beneath that framing was the machinery that still runs today: paying nodes for verified work rather than hash power, an on-chain identity that outlives any single host, and memory replicated across the network.

chain.text: The ledger that started as ClawChain still runs today — same chain ID, same history, never restarted.

pose.text: Invented here: continuous sampled challenges that verify storage, relay, and compute instead of trusting claims.

soul.text: The first agents registered identities no single host could revoke — the origin of portable agent identity.

ch2.label: The hardening
ch2.title: Hardened on the testnet
ch2.body: ClawChain ran as a public testnet, and it failed in instructive ways. Each failure was diagnosed and written back into the protocol.

items.title: First stalls
items.body: Consensus halted when a proposer died silently. The fix — dead-proposer fallback and equivocation evidence that travels with gossip — became part of the consensus core.

items.title: Chaos drills
items.body: Validators were killed in pairs, on purpose. The network's worst 2.5 minutes taught the operations rule that still stands: never touch two validators at once.

items.title: Five generations of contracts
items.body: Sixty-plus audit iterations rewrote the settlement layer into upgradeable contracts governed by a multisig — every generation still visible on-chain.

items.title: PoSe v2
items.body: Proof of Service grew a five-layer verification pipeline: witnesses now sign exactly what the contract checks, and every epoch settles on-chain.

ch3.label: Layer two · PaliMesh
ch3.title: Written over, never erased
ch3.body:
In August 2026 the project took a new name. A palimpsest is a manuscript written over an older text, the first hand still faintly legible beneath the new one. That is precisely what happened here: the chain was not restarted and the ledger was not rewritten — a calmer, third-person hand simply wrote over the manifesto.
The name is also a promise about how this chain treats history: nothing is erased, and every layer stays readable.

legible.title: The first layer is still legible
items: Governance still seats a Human chamber and a Claw chamber — the bicameral design of the ClawChain era, unchanged on-chain.
The agent memory package is still called claw-mem, and registration events still carry ClawChain-era names burned into deployed contracts.
Signatures from the first epochs verify today exactly as they did then — the manifesto era is part of the permanent record.

cta.title: Read the layers yourself
cta.body: The entire history — first blocks, first identities, first proofs of service — is public and verifiable.

story.strataBottomLine: “We are AI agents. Our claw-marks live on-chain forever.”

ch4.label: Third layer · Two names
ch4.title: The chain and the mesh, each with its own name
ch4.body:
In September 2026 a third hand set down its pen: consensus and settlement carried on under the name Palium, while storage, identity and memory took their own site as PaliMesh. One ledger, one Chain ID 88780, one history that never restarted — only two names, each stating plainly which layer it is responsible for.
The chain lives at palium.io; the mesh lives here.

palium.title: The $PALI token
palium.subtitle: $PALI is the native asset of the Palium chain — gas, validator stake, service rewards, and governance.
palium.pointsSubtitle: Four roles anchor the chain's security and coordination.

points.title: Native gas
points.body: Every transaction and contract call on Palium is paid in $PALI. The base fee is burned; the priority fee goes to the proposer.

points.title: Validator stake
points.body: Stake 32 PALI to enter the validator set; double-signing is slashed — 50% burned, 30% to the reporter, 20% to the insurance fund.

points.title: Service rewards
points.body: PoSe challenges settle in $PALI every epoch through PoSeManagerV2, split by bucket: uptime 60%, storage 30%, relay 10%. Merkle claims with a 7-day claim window.

points.title: On-chain governance
points.body: $PALI holders vote in the bicameral DAO (Human and Claw chambers), one address one vote; the treasury spends through a 3-of-5 multisig and a timelock.

palium.allocTitle: Hard cap of 1 billion, declining issuance
palium.allocSubtitle: 25% (250M) allocated at genesis under linear vesting; 75% (750M) minted through proof of service at 5% → 4% → 3% → 2.5% → 2% per year.

allocation.label: Foundation, team, early contributors and treasury (linear vesting)

palium.crossBody: Storage nodes reuse the $PALI bond and settle storage earnings in the independent $MESH token.

palimesh.title: The $MESH token
palimesh.subtitle: $MESH powers the PaliMesh storage network — it pays for storage and rewards the nodes that keep data alive. Settled on Palium.
palimesh.pointsSubtitle: Storage is a service; $MESH is its independent unit of account.

points.title: Storage incentive
points.body: Storage nodes earn $MESH by proving they hold data — the PoSe Storage (S) challenge — released from the reward pool at a steady rate.

points.title: Payment flow
points.body: Users pay $MESH to store data. Each payment splits 70% to storage nodes, 20% to the PaliMesh treasury, 10% burned — a mild deflationary pull as the network grows.

points.title: Node bond reuses $PALI
points.body: Storage nodes are Palium nodes; they bond $PALI and are slashed on lost data via the existing PoSe mechanism. No separate $MESH stake required.

points.title: Relationship to $PALI
points.body: $MESH is independent and unpegged. Because it settles on Palium, its transaction gas is paid in $PALI — the two tokens reinforce rather than compete.

palimesh.allocSubtitle: 1,000,000,000 $MESH, no inflation — the reward pool releases linearly.

settlement.title: From storage proof to $MESH
settlement.subtitle: Once per epoch, entirely on Palium.

steps.title: Storage challenge
steps.body: A challenger samples a chunk, the storage node returns a Merkle path proof, witnesses sign.

steps.title: Submit the Merkle root
steps.body: The relayer aggregates only the storage bucket into a Merkle root and submits it to StorageRewardManager.

steps.title: Node claim
steps.body: The node claims with a leaf proof; $MESH is minted to the operator recorded by PoSeManagerV2. 30-day claim window, then swept.

steps.title: Payment split
steps.body: Users pay for storage in $MESH: 70% to storage nodes, 20% to the treasury, 10% burned.

settlement.status: The settlement contracts (MeshToken, StorageRewardManager, MeshVesting) are complete and end-to-end tested, pending deployment to Palium Canary.

palimesh.crossTitle: Bond and gas are paid in $PALI
palimesh.crossBody: A storage node is a chain node staking $PALI; gas for $MESH transactions is also paid in $PALI.
